segments.text: Geomorphology explains how the Earth’s surface is created and reshaped. Some forces originate inside the Earth and build relief; other forces act at or near the surface and wear it down, transport material and deposit it elsewhere.
This is a process-based topic. If the process is understood, the landform becomes easy. Therefore study every subtopic with the sequence: cause → process → landform/effect → diagram/example.

items.text: Controls of landform development

: Landforms reflect rock type and structure, tectonic setting, climate, time, vegetation, water, ice, wind, gravity and human activity. The same process can produce different forms under different geological or climatic conditions.
Endogenic and exogenic forces

: Endogenic forces come from Earth’s internal energy and include tectonic movement, mountain building, volcanism and earthquakes. Exogenic processes operate mainly at the surface through weathering, mass movement, rivers, glaciers, wind, waves and groundwater.
Earth’s crust and interior

: Study crust, mantle and core, plus the mechanical idea of lithosphere and asthenosphere. The deeper Earth cannot be directly observed everywhere, so knowledge comes from seismic waves, material evidence and geophysical models.
Geosynclines

: Geosyncline theory is an older explanation of mountain-building involving long subsiding troughs of sediment. It remains in the syllabus for historical understanding, but modern geology explains large-scale mountain building mainly through plate tectonics.
Continental drift

: Alfred Wegener argued that continents had moved and were once joined. Evidence included matching continental shapes, fossils, rock belts and paleoclimate indicators. The original theory lacked a convincing mechanism, which later plate-tectonic evidence supplied.
Isostasy

: Isostasy is the idea of gravitational balance in which the lithosphere “floats” on denser underlying material. Thick continental or mountain roots and uplift after removal of ice or erosion can be explained through isostatic adjustment.
Sea-floor spreading and plate tectonics
: New oceanic crust forms at spreading ridges and is recycled at subduction zones. Plate tectonics unifies continental movement, ocean-floor spreading, earthquakes, volcanoes and many mountain belts.
Mountain building, volcanicity and earthquakes

: Convergence can thicken and fold crust to form mountains; magma reaching the surface produces volcanic activity; sudden release of accumulated strain along faults produces earthquakes. Their global distribution is strongly linked to plate boundaries.
Geomorphic cycles

: Classical geomorphic-cycle ideas describe landscape evolution through stages, but modern geomorphology recognizes that tectonics, climate and process rates can interrupt simple stage sequences. Present the classical model and then add this limitation.
Fluvial landforms
: Rivers erode, transport and deposit material. Common features include V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, meanders, floodplains, levees, oxbow lakes, deltas and alluvial fans.
Arid landforms
: Dry environments are shaped by mechanical weathering, wind and episodic water flow. Features can include dunes, deflation hollows, yardangs, wadis, pediments and alluvial fans.
Glacial landforms
: Glaciers erode through abrasion and plucking and deposit till and outwash. Common features include cirques, arêtes, U-shaped valleys, moraines, drumlins and eskers.
Coastal landforms
: Waves, currents, tides, rock resistance and sediment supply shape cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches, stacks, beaches, spits and bars.
Karst and groundwater

: Karst develops mainly where soluble rocks such as limestone are dissolved by slightly acidic water. Features include sinkholes, caves, stalactites and stalagmites. Groundwater moves through pores and fractures and is stored in aquifers.

blocks.text: Geomorphology as a system of structure, process and time

segments.text: Geomorphology explains landforms by combining three broad controls: the material and structure of the crust, the processes acting on that material, and the time over which those processes operate. A river valley, for example, cannot be explained by running water alone; rock resistance, uplift, climate, vegetation, sediment load and the history of the landscape all influence its form.

items.text: Structure
: Lithology, bedding, joints, faults and folds influence where erosion is rapid or slow. Resistant rocks may form ridges or cliffs, while weaker rocks are often lowered more quickly.
Process

: Endogenic processes deform or build relief through tectonics and volcanism. Exogenic processes weather, erode, transport and deposit material through water, wind, ice, waves, groundwater and gravity.
Time and equilibrium

: Landscapes are dynamic. They may adjust toward temporary equilibrium with prevailing conditions, but tectonic uplift, climate change or human disturbance can reset the system. This is why simple stage models are useful teaching tools but not complete descriptions of all real landscapes.

blocks.text: Earth structure, isostasy and the plate-tectonic framework

items.text: Crust, mantle and core

: The compositional model divides Earth into crust, mantle and core. The mechanical model distinguishes rigid lithosphere from the weaker asthenosphere below. Plate tectonics concerns movement of lithospheric plates.
Evidence from seismic waves

: Changes in seismic-wave speed and the behaviour of P and S waves reveal boundaries and material properties inside Earth. Because deep layers cannot be observed directly across the whole planet, geophysical inference is essential.
Isostasy

: Isostasy describes gravitational adjustment of the lithosphere relative to denser underlying material. Thick mountain belts can have deep roots, and removal of large ice loads can be followed by isostatic rebound over long periods.
Continental drift

: Wegener proposed that continents had once been joined and later separated. Fossil distributions, matching rock belts and paleoclimatic evidence supported mobility, but he lacked a convincing mechanism.
Sea-floor spreading

: Mid-ocean ridges create new oceanic lithosphere that moves away from spreading centres. Symmetrical magnetic patterns in oceanic crust and the age pattern of the sea floor provided major evidence for spreading.
Plate tectonics

: The modern framework links spreading, subduction and transform motion with global patterns of earthquakes, volcanoes, trenches, ridges and mountain belts. Plates move relative to one another; the boundaries concentrate much, though not all, tectonic activity.

blocks.text: Plate boundaries, mountain building, volcanism and earthquakes

items.text: Divergent boundaries
: Plates separate and new crust forms, as at mid-ocean ridges and continental rifts. Extension produces normal faulting, volcanism and shallow earthquakes.
Convergent boundaries

: Plates move together. Oceanic lithosphere may subduct, generating trenches, volcanic arcs and deep-to-shallow earthquake zones. Continent-continent collision thickens crust and contributes to large mountain systems.
Transform boundaries
: Plates slide laterally past one another. Crust is neither created nor destroyed at the boundary, but accumulated strain can produce powerful shallow earthquakes.
Orogeny

: Mountain building involves crustal shortening, folding, faulting, metamorphism, magmatism and uplift over geological time. Mountains therefore record tectonic history rather than forming in one event.
Volcanoes

: Volcanic form depends on magma composition, viscosity, gas content and eruption style. Basaltic lava tends to be less viscous, while silica-rich magma is often more viscous and can support explosive eruption.
Earthquakes

: Earthquakes result from sudden slip along faults after elastic strain accumulates. Magnitude measures released energy, while intensity describes observed effects at places and therefore varies with distance, ground conditions and building vulnerability.
Mechanical weathering
: Breaks rock without changing its chemical composition. Temperature change, freeze-thaw action, salt growth and unloading can contribute under suitable conditions.
Chemical weathering
: Alters minerals through reactions such as solution, oxidation, hydration and hydrolysis. Warm, wet conditions often accelerate chemical processes.
Biological influence
: Roots, burrowing organisms and organic acids can contribute to physical disruption and chemical alteration.
Mass movement

: Gravity moves weathered material downslope through rockfall, landslide, slump, debris flow or slow creep. Water often reduces friction or adds weight, while slope angle, geology and vegetation affect stability.
Erosion
: Hydraulic action, abrasion and solution deepen or widen channels. Dominant processes vary with discharge, gradient, sediment and rock resistance.
Transport
: Rivers move dissolved load, suspended load and bed load. Competence concerns the largest particle a stream can transport; capacity concerns total sediment load.
Upper-course forms
: Steep gradients encourage vertical erosion, producing V-shaped valleys, rapids and waterfalls where geological conditions permit.
Meanders
: Helicoidal flow and differing velocity encourage outer-bank erosion and inner-bank deposition. Meanders can migrate laterally and eventually form oxbow lakes when a neck is cut through.
Floodplains and levees
: Repeated overbank deposition builds floodplains. Coarser material is often deposited near the channel margins during floods, contributing to natural levees.
Deltas and alluvial fans
: Deposition occurs where transport capacity falls. Deltas develop where river sediment supply exceeds marine removal near a coast; alluvial fans form where steep streams emerge onto gentler plains.

blocks.text: Arid, glacial, coastal and karst systems

items.text: Arid geomorphology

: Drylands experience limited vegetation, strong physical weathering, wind action and episodic high-energy runoff. Dunes, yardangs, desert pavements, wadis and alluvial fans reflect different combinations of wind and water.
Glacial erosion
: Moving ice erodes by abrasion and plucking, creating cirques, arêtes, horns and U-shaped valleys. Erosional form depends on ice thickness, basal conditions and rock structure.
Glacial deposition
: Till is unsorted material deposited directly by ice; meltwater deposits are better sorted. Moraines, drumlins and eskers record different depositional processes.
Coastal erosion
: Wave energy, geology, sediment supply and sea-level conditions shape cliffs, platforms, caves, arches and stacks. Refraction concentrates energy on headlands and can reduce it in bays.
Coastal deposition
: Longshore transport can build beaches, spits and bars when sediment supply and wave conditions permit. Coastal forms are therefore parts of sediment cells rather than isolated features.
Karst

: Carbon dioxide dissolves in water to create weak carbonic acid, which dissolves calcium carbonate in limestone. Jointed, permeable limestone can develop sinkholes, disappearing streams, caves and depositional features such as stalactites and stalagmites.

blocks.text: Classical geomorphic cycles and modern caution

segments.text: William Morris Davis proposed a cycle of youth, maturity and old age after uplift. The model was historically influential because it organized landform evolution as a sequence. Modern geomorphology, however, recognizes that uplift can continue, climate can change, process rates can vary and landscapes can be polycyclic. In an examination answer, explain the classical logic and then state why real landscapes need not pass through a single orderly sequence.
Reading the flow: each step creates the conditions for the next; the arrows show sequence or influence, not inevitability unless the text explicitly says so.

rows: Avoid this error Do not memorize landform names without explaining how they form. In Geography, a labelled process diagram often earns more clarity than a long descriptive paragraph.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Open with geomorphology and controls, explain internal Earth and tectonic theories, then organize surface landforms by agent—river, wind/arid, glacier, coast, karst—and finish with the interaction of tectonics and denudation.

• Endogenic forces build or deform relief; exogenic processes weather, erode, move and deposit material.
• Plate tectonics connects continental drift, sea-floor spreading, mountain belts, earthquakes and volcanism.
• Landforms reflect both process and geological/climatic setting.
• Groundwater is stored and transmitted through permeable geological material, especially aquifers.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
